summary: Supply the thermal conductivity constant, the temperature difference and the heat flux and the Thermal conductivity calculator solves for distance (Δx). Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Thermal conductivity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Thermal conductivity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports distance (Δx) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the thermal conductivity constant (λ), the temperature difference (ΔT) and the heat flux (q).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in watts per meter-kelvin. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 8 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in watts per meter squared. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Thermal conductivity calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Distance (Δx)=-thermal conductivity constant (λ) × temperature difference (ΔT) ÷ heat flux (q)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Thermal conductivity constant (λ) = 10 W/(m·K), Temperature difference (ΔT) = 10 °C and Heat flux (q) = 10 W/m². The calculator returns Distance (Δx) = -1000 m.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Distance (Δx) = -1000 m should be roughly the size you expected from Thermal conductivity constant (λ) = 10 W/(m·K) and Temperature difference (ΔT) = 10 °C.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Thermal conductivity, opening in watts per meter-kelvin
  • Temperature change, opening in Celsius
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Power per area, opening in watts per meter squared

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Thermal conductivity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the thermal conductivity constant, the temperature difference and the heat flux — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Thermal conductivity calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Thermal conductivity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns distance (Δx), derived from the thermal conductivity constant, the temperature difference and the heat flux. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Thermal conductivity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the thermal conductivity constant, the temperature difference and the heat flux, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter thermal conductivity constant (λ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Thermal conductivity constant (λ) opens in watts per meter-kelvin and the chip beside it offers 2 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Distance (Δx) = -1000 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Thermal conductivity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
